note: The 24 checkpoint-after-flow documents judged in one sitting immediately after the before set (2026-09-08-rejudge-checkpoint-before-3.json); compare `now` against that file.

then.rationale: Integrity holds page to page — no clipping, no placeholder text, and the running head, footer rule and page numbers repeat identically on pages 2–4. Type is legible: body copy on pages 2–3 sits at a comfortable reading size, headings are clearly differentiated by weight and the blue rule under 'The problem is not price alone' and 'Recommendation: premiumise...' repeats consistently, so levels 1–3 are met. It fails at level 4 mainly on page 4, which carries only the three-word orphan 'research already in hand.' plus a 'Notes and sources' list with a single footnote — roughly four fifths of the page is empty, so the last page reads as a spill rather than a closing section. Communicatively the titles do work (each heading on pages 2 and 3 states a conclusion, not a topic), and the stat row on page 3 (-4pts / 38% / 61%) carries units, labels and a source line 'Internal share tracking and consumer research, 2026'. But the core of the brief — two repositioning options weighed against each other — is delivered on page 2 as two undifferentiated paragraphs under 'Two credible paths, not one obvious answer' with no comparison table or any device that lets the marketing director see the trade-off at a glance; pages 2 and 3 are near-uninterrupted grey text columns. The one break in rhythm, the boxed 'About this assessment' aside on page 2, is method commentary rather than argument. Page 1 is also thin: title, subtitle, date and confidentiality line float in the upper third with the lower two thirds blank. Visually it is a competent but standard report shell — thin blue rules, single text column, small caps running head — that would look identical for a telecoms or pharma assessment; only the stat callouts on page 3 feel authored for this brief.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text, and the cover on page 1 (eyebrow 'Marketing Director', title, subtitle, date, 'Client Confidential') is complete. Type is legible and reading order is single-column and obvious. Coherence is largely maintained — consistent rule under each H2 ('The situation', 'Two paths forward', 'Recommendation', 'What would change this recommendation'), a consistent running head and three-part footer. It stops at level 3 because communicative effectiveness fails in two visible places. First, the A/B comparison table starts on page 2 with its header row ('Dimension | A - Narrow the gap | B - Premiumise') and continues at the top of page 3 with the 'Margin, 3 years' and 'Risk if wrong' rows and no repeated header, so on page 3 the two columns are unlabelled and the reader cannot tell which option each cell belongs to. Second, page 4 carries only three bullets finishing the evidence list plus a one-line 'Notes and sources', leaving roughly two-thirds of the page empty — a break that should have been avoided or absorbed. The stat trio on page 3 (38% price gap, -4pts share, 61% growth) is the strongest element and correctly carries units, arrows and a source line beneath it. Genericness is middling: the structure and quiet rule-and-serif-free treatment would suit any strategy memo, with nothing about a 90-year-old food brand in the palette or composition, but the stat band, the 'How to read the price gap' explainer box and the option table are shaped by this specific argument rather than generic filler.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder content, and the four pages render fully. Legibility is acceptable in the body, though the page-1 metadata block ('8 September 2026 / Client Confidential') is set very small relative to everything else. Coherence is largely there — consistent running head, footer with page numbers and date, blue rule under each H2, consistent left-aligned single column. Where it breaks down is communicative effectiveness. Page 4 is the clearest failure: it holds only two short paragraphs and a one-line 'Notes and sources' list, then roughly two-thirds of the page is blank, so the document ends on a near-empty leaf rather than a designed close. Page 2 is the opposite problem — 'Over three years...' and the two paragraphs under 'Two paths, two different businesses' are unbroken walls of running text with no pull-out, table or figure to carry the option comparison, which is the central decision in the brief. The only visual device in the entire document is the three-stat row on page 3 ('4 pts / 38% / 61%'), and it sits below the recommendation it is meant to support rather than leading it; the '4 pts' and '61%' captions carry units but the source line under it is a generic 'Source: retail category audit and brand consumer research, 2026' with no methodology tie to the 'Method note' paragraph directly above on the same page. Two options that the brief frames as a fork are never shown side by side — no comparison table, no framing of volume-vs-margin trade-off in any visual form. Headings do argue ('The situation is a slow leak, not a single wound', 'Recommend premiumising, not price-matching') which is the strongest thing here. Distinctiveness is thin: a blue accent rule, a blue eyebrow, one stat row — nothing that reads as built for a 90-year-old heritage food brand rather than any consulting memo. I would not send this with my name on it, mostly because of the abandoned page 4 and the missing options comparison.

Integrity is mostly intact — no clipped or overflowing text, no lorem placeholders — but page 2 and page 3 each carry a small orphaned mark near the top of the text column (a stray glyph directly under the running head and above 'The programme is EUR 9 million behind plan at month fourteen', and again above 'Three decisions recover half the shortfall this quarter'), and the same stray sits again mid-column on page 2 above 'Property and IT are blocked on decisions, not on delivery'. Those read as unrendered or empty block markers rather than intentional rules. Legibility holds: single measure, dark type on white, generous leading, obvious reading order, consistent running head 'Cost Programme Review' and footer 'Confidential — Transformation Office / p / September 2026'. Coherence is respectable — the blue accent recurs on the cover rule, the section-title underline and the KPI figures on page 3 — so the level 3 bar is met at the seam. It does not reach level 4. The brief asks the document to name three decisions and their owners, and page 3 sets up '3 — Decisions required' as a KPI, then delivers the substance as a single unbroken paragraph ('The first decision is the office footprint consolidation... The third is procedural...') with no table, no owner column, no dates. That is exactly the content that should have been a decision table with owner and deadline, and it is the one element a transformation office would act from. Similarly the 41% / 33% / 118% workstream performance — the analytical spine of the brief — appears only as prose on page 2 under 'Property and IT are blocked'; there is no chart or table anywhere in the document, so there is nothing to attach a takeaway or source to. The KPI strip on page 3 ('9.0 €m Shortfall vs. plan / 4.5 €m Recoverable this quarter / 3 Decisions required') is the only piece of real information design and it is good — units present, labels present, a source line beneath it. Page 2 is a wall of body text with one bulleted 'Key takeaways' and one small 'Why this matters' callout; density is uniform and undifferentiated for a three-page executive review. On genericness: the titles are genuinely argued rather than generic ('Property and IT are blocked on decisions, not on delivery', 'Unchanged, the programme lands at EUR 33 million') and that is the strongest thing here, but the container — thin blue rule over a left-aligned cover block, one accent colour, default serif-free body, no distinctive grid — would look identical for any other consulting review with the words swapped. I would not send this unchanged: the decisions and owners need to be a scannable table, and the stray marks at the top of pages 2 and 3 would need removing first.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, the KPI strip on page 2 (68%, 118%, 41%, 33% with delta pills), the grouped bar chart on page 3 and the three-row 'Value at stake' table all render fully. Legibility is fine — body text is a comfortable size, headings are clearly ranked, and the single-column reading order is unambiguous. Coherence also holds: the running head 'Cost Programme Review — Month 14', the footer triplet (Confidential / page x-4 / 8 September 2026), the blue rule under each H1 and the small 'Source: Programme Management Office...' line under both the chart and the table repeat identically. Where it fails is level 4, density fitting purpose: page 2 ends after a three-line paragraph under 'Where the shortfall sits' and leaves roughly the bottom 45% of the page blank, and page 4 stops after 'Notes and sources' with about a quarter of the page empty — a four-page document with this much air reads as one-section-per-page pagination rather than a composed spread, and the shortfall argument on page 2 is starved (three lines) while a full half-page sat available beside it. Section headings are also locational rather than conclusive: 'Where the shortfall sits', 'If nothing changes' and 'Recommendation' name the topic but the number that matters (EUR 33m landing vs EUR 46m target, EUR 13m permanent shortfall) is buried in the body rather than in the title. Positives worth noting for level 4 partially met: the chart caption on page 3 does carry a takeaway ('Procurement is running ahead of target; property and IT are under half'), and every figure carries a unit or an explicit basis. The shell itself — thin blue rule, sans headings, plain KPI row — is the standard transformation-office briefing dressing and would look identical for a supply-chain or IT review; only the content, not the composition, is specific to this programme.

Integrity and legibility hold: nothing on pages 1–3 is clipped or overflowing, the running head ("Cost Programme Review — Month 14") and footer ("Confidential — Programme Board" / page number / date) repeat identically on pages 2 and 3, body type is comfortably readable and the single-column reading order is unambiguous. (A stray two-character mark sits just above "Where the programme stands" on page 2 under the rule; it is small enough that it does not drive the level, but it looks like an unrendered heading marker and should be checked.) Coherence is met: the blue keyline under every H2, the same left-aligned heading scale and the same body measure carry across pages 2 and 3, and the "Method note" callout on page 2 is styled as a deliberate variant rather than a hand-placed box.

Level 4 is not met on three specific counts. First, the whole delivery story is four workstreams against target (118%, 41%, 33%, plus the EUR 19m vs EUR 28m plan) and there is no table or chart anywhere — page 2 carries it entirely in prose, and page 3's stat row shows only Property and IT, so Procurement's 118% overperformance and the 19-vs-28 gap never appear in any comparable visual form. Second, the page 3 stat row breaks the unit rule: "41" and "33" are bare integers with no % sign; the unit only appears indirectly in the "-59 pts" / "-67 pts" deltas and the "Property vs target" / "IT vs target" captions. The third figure, "2 — Minimum months blocked", is a different kind of quantity sitting in the same row with the same visual weight, which flattens the hierarchy. Third, page 2's headings "What is working" and "What is blocking the rest" are section labels, not conclusions — page 3's "What this quarter's decisions are worth" shows the document knows how to write a conclusion-bearing title and the earlier two do not follow it.

The brief's hardest asks are actually satisfied: page 3 names three decisions with named owners (Chief Operating Officer, Chief Information Officer, Programme Sponsor/Transformation Office) and page 2 states the do-nothing landing point explicitly. Sourcing is present on both the stat row and in "Notes and sources". Against that, page 1 is a cover with roughly three quarters of the page empty below "Confidential — Programme Board", which in a three-page board memo spends a third of the document on a title block. I would not send this unchanged: I would add a workstream-vs-target table, put % on the 41 and 33, and either fill or drop the cover.

On genericness: the content is unmistakably this brief, but the composition is not. Strip the words and this is a title page, a rule-under-heading text page and a stat row — the one distinctive element is the three-up figure block on page 3, and it is a common pattern. Nothing in the type, colour (a single accent blue) or layout would change if the subject were a supply-chain review instead of a cost programme.

Integrity holds: no clipped or empty frames, the running head ("CSRD Readiness Assessment") and footer ("Confidential: Audit Committee Only / page / 3 September 2026") repeat on every page, and the tier table that breaks between pages 3 and 4 repeats its "Tier | Count | Share (%)" header on page 4. Legibility is fine and reading order is single-column and obvious. Coherence is good: the same blue rule under section headings, consistent margins, and one heading scale across pages 2-5. Communication is genuinely strong for the brief — the 34/82, 29/82, 19/82 stat trio on page 2 carries labels and a source line, the page 3 bar chart has a numbered figure caption with an actual takeaway ("Tier 2 is the year's real work") plus "Internal datapoint gap assessment, September 2026", and headings such as "What the First Report Will Not Be Able to Say" state conclusions rather than topics. What stops me sending it: the datapoint tier table is orphaned at the very bottom of page 3 with only the Tier 1 row before the break, so page 4 opens cold with two stray table rows above the "Note on the build plan" box; page 5 carries only the recommendation paragraph and a one-item "Notes and sources" list, leaving roughly two thirds of the page blank; the title page fills only the top third; and there are small stray glyphs sitting alone under the running head on pages 2, 4 and 5 (and mid-column on page 2) that read as leftover markers rather than design. On genericness, the copy is specific to this mandate but the shell — blue-on-white headings, one plain single-series bar chart with a redundant "Datapoints (of 82)" legend, and the placeholder-sounding "The Company" brand line on page 1 — would look identical for any audit-committee memo.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, body copy is readable at print size, and the running head ("CSRD Readiness Assessment") / footer ("Confidential — Audit Committee | p/5 | 4 September 2026") repeat identically on pages 2–5. Coherence is also good — the blue rule under every H2, the grey callout boxes ("Method note", "Assurance risk" on p4), and the caption/source pairing all repeat consistently. Content-level craft is above average for the brief: the p2 stat band (82 / 34 / 29 / 19 with labels), the p3 figure caption that states a conclusion ("The gap is not half-bounded: 19 datapoints need new measurement capability, not all 82"), the % share column in the p3 table, and section titles that assert rather than label ("Scope 3 Emissions: The Critical Gap", "What the First Report Will Honestly Not Be Able to Say"). What blocks level 4 is density and page rhythm across 3 of 5 pages. Page 1 is a near-empty cover: a title, subtitle, date and confidentiality line sitting in the upper third with roughly two-thirds of the sheet blank and nothing else — no client, no contents, no framing number. Page 3 stops after the source line under the readiness table with about a quarter of the page left empty. Page 4 is worse: "What to Estimate, and How to Label It" gets a heading and one paragraph, then a large white gap to the footer, and the same section resumes at the top of page 5 ("We recommend the committee approve a short estimation policy now...") — a mid-section break with a hole in it reads as a forced page break, not a decision. Also, the p3 bar chart is a three-bar column with a redundant one-item legend ("ESRS datapoints") that adds nothing the axis title doesn't already say. Fix the p4 gap, fill or rethink the cover, and this reaches 4. Genericness: the prose and headings are unmistakably written for this brief, but the chassis — plain cover, single column, stat band, one bar chart, one table — would look identical for any other assessment memo.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text on any of the three pages, and the page-2 'Governance note' callout and page-3 big-number band both render cleanly. Legibility is the first real weakness — the body text on pages 2 and 3 is set very small relative to the wide single-column measure, and the running head/footer rules are so light they barely register; still readable, so level 2 passes, marginally. Visual coherence is met: consistent left-aligned rule under each H2, consistent running head 'CSRD Readiness Assessment' and footer, and the cover on page 1 uses the same type family and eyebrow treatment. Level 4 fails: the only quantitative display in the whole document is the page-3 '34/82, 29/82, 19/82' number band, and it carries no chart at all — the three-tier gap analysis that is the entire analytical spine of the brief (34 collected / 29 collectable / 19 new) is delivered as running prose plus one numeric strip, with no table listing which datapoints sit in which tier, no timeline for what to build first, and no visualisation of Scope 3 as the single largest gap. Titles do conclude ('Two in five required datapoints are already reporting-ready', 'Build the missing 19 datapoints first', 'The first report should disclose its limits'), which is a genuine strength, but the page-3 number band's source line is set in a grey so light it is nearly illegible, and there is no unit statement for whether 82 is datapoints or disclosures anywhere near it. Page 3 also ends with a single-item 'Notes and sources' list citing only 'Internal ESRS datapoint gap assessment, August 2026', which is thin evidence for an audit committee document. Genericness: the headline writing is clearly specific to this brief, but the shell — cover with rule, one column of grey body text, one number strip — would look identical for any three-page memo on any topic; nothing in the layout is doing CSRD-specific work.

Integrity mostly holds — no clipped text, no visible placeholder strings, the table on page 3 fits its column, and the three-up stat row (2.1 €m / 26 mo / 34 mo) sits cleanly on the grid. The one concern is a stray dark glyph that appears immediately under the running head on both page 2 and page 3, and again between the payback table and the 'Conditions for the Recommendation' heading on page 3; it is too small to read but it is not part of any labelled element and reads as a leftover marker. Legibility is fine: body type is consistent, the blue rules under 'Recommendation', 'Market Opportunity', 'Investment Case and Payback' and 'Conditions for the Recommendation' give an unambiguous reading order, and the 'Key takeaways' and 'Definition' boxes are tinted lightly enough to keep contrast. Coherence is the strongest level: running head, folio and date repeat identically on pages 2 and 3, heading rules are the same weight and colour, and the stat row, table and source lines all align to the same measure. It falls short at communicative effectiveness. Every heading is a topic label rather than a conclusion — 'Market Opportunity' and 'Investment Case and Payback' say nothing the board could not guess, whereas the cover subtitle ('Should the Client Open a Stockholm Sales Office in FY27?') shows the document knows how to phrase a question but never answers it in a heading. The payback under both cases, which is the analytic centre of the brief, is delivered only as a two-row table; the sentence 'The table below sets out the payback timeline for each scenario' promises a timeline that is never drawn, so the 26- vs 34-month gap is left for the reader to picture. Page 1 is also badly under-filled: title, subtitle, date and 'Confidential — Board Use Only' occupy roughly the middle third and the bottom half is blank with no device to close it. On genericness, strip the Nordic nouns and this is an unmarked consulting memo shell — thin blue rule, grey running head, tinted callout, three big numbers — that would render identically for a supply-chain or pricing brief.

Integrity and legibility hold: nothing is clipped or overlapping, the running head ("Nordic Market Entry Assessment"), the blue rule under each section heading and the Confidential / page x of x / date footer repeat identically on pages 2-4, and the reading order is unambiguous. Body type, the KPI trio on page 3 (2.1 €m / 26 mo / 34 mo with captions and a "Company financial model, FY2027 planning case" source line) and the Payback table (units carried in the headers: Invest. €m, Window (mo), Breakeven (mo), plus a footnote on the pessimistic row) all read cleanly. Coherence is genuinely good — one grid, one accent colour, one heading scale across all four pages. It fails at level 4 on density and page economy. Page 4 is a stub: a single four-line "Risks to Monitor" paragraph and a one-item "Notes and sources" list, leaving roughly three quarters of the sheet blank, and the two named risks (incumbent Finnish-language response, procurement cycle length) are buried in prose rather than broken out for a board. Page 3 stops around 60% down, so the section-per-page rhythm is paying for itself in white space rather than structure. The brief asks to "show the payback under both cases" and there is no visual at all — a two-row table is the only treatment, so the month-26 vs month-34 gap and the four-year window are never made visible. Section titles are also labels rather than conclusions: "Investment and Payback" and "Risks to Monitor" state the topic, not the finding, whereas the deck's actual conclusion (Stockholm office, Finnish-language product, break-even inside the planning horizon) only appears in body copy. Small stray marks sit under the running head on pages 2 and 3 and between the boxed recommendation and "Market Opportunity" on page 2 — they read as orphaned footnote references with nothing visible attached. Not something I would send to a board over my own name without collapsing pages 3-4 and giving the payback a chart.

Genericness: the content is unmistakably this brief — EUR 340m, 61% incumbent share, the Finnish-language gap, the Stockholm office — and the KPI trio plus the Note callout on page 2 are more than a bare template offers. But the chrome (thin blue rule, sans heads, three-part footer, near-empty title page with an eyebrow) would look identical for any consulting memo on any topic; nothing about the composition is specific to a market-entry decision.

Integrity holds: no clipped or empty regions on any of the three pages, the running head, footer rule with page numbers and date repeat identically on pages 2 and 3, and the cover's accent rule above 'Board of Directors' picks up the same colour as the section heading treatment. Legibility is fine at print size and the reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is met — headings, the 'Market structure' callout on page 2 and the KPI band on page 3 all sit on the same left margin and share type ramp. It stops at level 3 because the brief's explicit ask — show the payback under both cases — is answered only by three bare figures (€2.1m / 26 mo / 34 mo) in the page 3 KPI band; there is no payback curve, no month-by-month table, nothing that lets a board see the eight-month gap between base and pessimistic rather than read about it in the paragraph beneath. The whole document contains zero charts and zero tables, so market size, 9% growth, the 61% incumbent share and the Finnish-language gap on page 2 all arrive as undifferentiated prose: page 2 is four full-measure paragraphs plus one callout, the least scannable page of the three for a board audience. Line measure on page 2 also runs the full A4 width, which hurts an already dense page. Titles are the strongest element — 'A EUR 340m Market Growing Faster Than It Is Defended' and 'Entry Costs EUR 2.1m and Breaks Even Within Three Years' state conclusions rather than topics — and page 3 does carry a note and a numbered source. Not sendable unchanged: I would have to build the payback comparison before putting my name on it.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no overflow, no placeholder text on any of the four pages; running head and footer ("Confidential — Steering Committee", "x / 4", date) repeat identically on pages 2–4. Legibility is fine — body copy is small but comfortable for A4 reading, the tinted summary block on page 2 and the callout "Overlap is not redundancy" both keep dark text on light tint, and reading order is single-column and unambiguous. Coherence is the strongest layer: the same heading-with-rule device opens every section ("Executive Summary", "Network Overlap and Rationalization", "Synergy Value...", "Recommended Sequencing", "Six-Month Milestones", "Cost of a One-Year Deferral"), margins and leading are constant, and the numbered milestone list on page 4 sits on the same grid as body text. It fails at level 4 on several counts. First, the stat trio on page 3 renders the currency as "8.2€m", "4.9€m", "3.3€m" — symbol after the number, which is malformed and inconsistent with "EUR 8.2 million" used in the running prose two lines above. Second, every section title is a topic label rather than a conclusion: "Synergy Value and the Dispatch System Dependency" names the subject but does not say that 40% of the synergy is hostage to an unbudgeted migration, which is the actual finding. Third, a brief built entirely on phasing (60% in eighteen months, three parallel streams, month 6/12/18 gates, a one-year deferral cost) is delivered with zero timeline, table or chart — the month-6/12/18 milestones on page 4 are a plain numbered list where a three-column gate table or a phasing bar would carry the sequence far better, and the deferral cost on page 4 is argued only in prose. Fourth, density is uneven: page 1 places all cover content in the top third and leaves two-thirds blank, and page 4 stops just past the midpoint, so the deferral argument — the sharpest point in the document — ends in half a page of white. On distinctiveness, the only element that could not be lifted wholesale into any other consulting report is the number trio on page 3; the eyebrow rule, section rules, tinted summary block, pull-quote callout and notes-and-sources footer are a stock professional-services kit, and nothing in the typography or colour (single navy accent on white) is chosen for a facilities-management merger specifically.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text on any of the four pages; the running head ("Post-Merger Integration Assessment"), the three-part footer ("Confidential — Committee Only" / page number / date) and the rule-over-heading treatment repeat identically on pages 2–4, and the title page's accent rule matches the heading rules, so the grid and typography agree throughout. That earns level 3.

It stops there on communicative effectiveness. (a) Page fill is ragged in a way that reads as unmanaged rather than deliberate: page 3 ends after a single paragraph under "Six-Month Milestones" with roughly the bottom third blank, and page 4 stops after the one-item "Notes and sources" list with nearly half the page empty — the milestones section is orphaned across the page 3/4 break with the heading stranded above the fold. (b) The two things the brief most needed as structure are delivered as prose: "Recommended Sequence" on page 3 is a single running paragraph enumerating months 1–6, 6–12, 12–18 with no numbered list, phasing table or timeline, and "Six-Month Milestones" is likewise a paragraph rather than named, checkable milestones. For a steering committee that has to approve a funding decision, a sequence with no visual sequence is the wrong instrument. (c) There is no table or chart anywhere in four pages — the 31% customer overlap, 12-of-41 depots and the 60/40 synergy split all live inside body text; the only quantified display is the three-stat row on page 3 (8.2€m / 60% / 40%), which does at least carry a source line ("Source: Integration business case, September 2026"). (d) The stat "8.2€m" sets the currency symbol after the number and before the magnitude suffix, which is not a form anyone writes — "EUR 8.2m" is used correctly in the body, so the display figure contradicts the prose. (e) Section titles are topic labels ("Integration Scope and Overlap", "Recommended Sequence", "The Cost of Deferring the System Migration") rather than statements of what the section concludes; the one conclusion-shaped element, the "Why the split matters" callout on page 3, shows the document knows how to do it and then doesn't.

Genericness: the callout box, the stat row and the thin accent rules give it a little more character than a bare Word default, but the system is the neutral consulting-report shell — swap the strings and this is an assessment of anything. Nothing in the layout is shaped by depots, dispatch systems or a phased migration; the one place the subject could have driven form (a sequence/timeline) is prose.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, overlap or placeholder copy, body type is comfortably readable, and the single-column reading order is unambiguous on every page. Coherence is real — the blue rule + running head 'Post-Merger Integration Assessment' and the 'Confidential – Committee Only / p / 8 September 2026' footer repeat identically on pages 2–5, the stat trio on page 2 (31%, 12/41, 8.2€m) and page 5 (3.28€m, 10–15%, 12) share the same numeral-plus-caption treatment, and heading scale and blue accent are consistent throughout. Communicative effectiveness is the document's strength: the page 3 chart carries a conclusion title ('Depot network overlap: 12 of 41 depots duplicate customer coverage'), a takeaway line ('the priority is dispatch consolidation, not site closure') and a dated source; the synergy table states its unit in the caption ('EUR millions') and splits 4.92/3.28 against the dependency; the brief's four asks (sequence, six-month milestones, deferral cost, funding gap) each get a named section, and the 'Funding gap' and 'Red flag' callouts on page 4 carry the argument rather than decorate it. What blocks level 5 and blocks shipping unchanged: the synergy table breaks so that only the repeated header and the 'Total identified synergy 8.20 / 100%' row land alone at the top of page 4, stranded above its own source caption — a two-line orphan that reads as a mistake; page 1 is a title block in the top third with the remaining two-thirds empty and no visual device at all; page 5 stops two-thirds down after 'Notes and sources'; the page 3 chart carries a one-item legend ('Depots') that says nothing the axis has not already said; and there are small stray glyph marks in the left margin under the running head on pages 2, 3, 4 and 5 (and twice on 5) that look like anchor artifacts. On genericness: the words are specific to this deal, but the dressing — thin blue rule, centred-caption stat row, default vertical bars, one column start to finish — would transfer unchanged to any other advisory memo.

Integrity holds: no clipped or overflowing frames, no placeholder text, and the 'Repricing targets and timing by tier' table that breaks between p3 and p4 repeats its 'Tier | Increase | Effective by' header on p4, so nothing is orphaned unreadably. Legibility is fine at letter size — body copy on p2/p4 is a comfortable measure, the blue accent on the p1 title rule and the p2 KPI row holds contrast against white. Coherence is consistent: same running head ('Pricing Review: Restoring Margin...'), same footer triplet (Confidential — Internal Only / page / September 2026), same heading weight and blue-rule treatment on all four pages. Communicative effectiveness is the strongest layer: every heading states a conclusion rather than a topic ('Margin has fallen twelve points in three years of frozen pricing', 'Three tiers, sequenced over nine months, protect the top of the book', 'The two largest accounts need a different playbook than a notice'), the p2 KPI row carries units (19% gross margin today, -12 pts, 22% cost inflation), the p3 bar chart has a Figure 1 caption that states the takeaway and a dated source line, the p4 table has a source note, and the 'Expected churn' callout on p4 quantifies 15–20% / 5–8% / 4–6% by tier — every brief requirement (segmentation, three tiers, nine-month runway, churn, largest-account refusal) is visibly answered. It stops short of level 5 on craft: the p1 cover is a bare title, subtitle and date against a large empty lower two-thirds with nothing anchoring it; the p3 chart is default-styled with a redundant legend swatch for a single series; and the table on p3 begins with only its header plus one 'Tier 1: Below cost' row before the break, which is a hand-placed-looking lapse rather than a deliberate composition. Not generic in argument — the titles could not be transplanted to another brief — but the visual system (blue rule, three-stat band, grey callout box) would look identical for any consulting report.

Integrity and legibility mostly hold — running heads, page numbers and date repeat on pages 2–6, the blue accent rule under every H2 is consistent, and the FY2023–FY2025 bar chart on page 3 carries both a takeaway caption ("Gross margin fell from 31% to 19%…") and a source line, as do both tables on pages 4 and 5. But two visible defects stop it below level 4. First, page 6 is a stub: three bullets and a four-item "Notes and sources" list occupy roughly the top sixth, leaving the rest of the sheet blank — the document ends on an orphan page rather than a finished one. Second, the "Recommended Next Steps" block straddling pages 5–6 repeats itself verbatim: the intro line "Approve the three-tier structure and the nine-month runway this month, and begin Tier 1 notices within two weeks" is restated word-for-word as the first bullet directly beneath it.
